newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Turkey spat over grain shipments still lingering.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Turkey spat over grain shipments still lingering.

text.p: U.S. grain shipments to Turkey are being held up as officials try to settle a lingering disagreement between the two nations over Turkey's strict import regulations.

An Agriculture Department official said Wednesday that despite Turkey's recent agreement to ease restrictions on the wheat ergot fungus, Turkey is insisting that imported grain and oilseeds be completely free of six other diseases.

Washington says it cannot make such iron-clad guarantees, and U.S. grain inspectors are continuing to withhold the issuing of export certificates for all grains and oilseed shipments to Turkey until the issue is settled.

"Right now Turkey would like us to certify that the grain is free of a number of diseases that we can't guarantee it is free of," said an official with the Agriculture Department's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.
"The ergot issue has been settled, but there's still other problems remaining ... there are no (export certificates) for any type of grains (and oilseeds) being issued to Turkey," said the official.

Turkey was originally insisting that Washington guarantee a zero content level for a number of bacterial and fungal diseases. That list has been whittled down to six diseases Turkey is most concerned about.

The United States is a main supplier of grain to Turkey, and a chief political ally. The current dispute flared up late last month when Turkey suddenly began imposing strict new import regulations that U.S. and other global agricultural exporters said were unrealistic and impossible to meet.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman met with the Turkish Ambassador to the United States last week in an attempt to settle the issue, and at that time stressed that the strict standards would impact not only shipments from the United States, but from other exporting nations as well.
Turkey is expected to import more than two million metric tons of wheat this year.
Turkey this week agreed to allow wheat shipments with a 0.05 percent content of the ergot wheat fungus, but has so far dug in its heels on this last handful of diseases.
A U.S. official said U.S. and Turkish plant quarantine officials are in discussions, and that hopefully the issue will be resolved soon.

In a press conference with reporters Wednesday from Rome, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he got the impression from his meeting with the Turkish ambassador that Turkey would be changing its import regulations fairly soon to come more in line with international norms.

"I got the clear impression that since the Turkish position was so outside the international norm on sanitary and phytosanitary standards that we would likely see some sort of a change fairly soon, but I have not discussed it any further since then," Glickman said.
